title: Poetry & Prosody
subtitle: Scan French verse, hear its rhymes, and read poems like a native

lessons.title: Le vers français
lessons.description: Learn to count syllables, scan the alexandrin, and recognise the classic French rhyme schemes.

blocks.heading: Compter les syllabes
blocks.body: French verse is measured in syllables, not stressed beats. The tricky part is the "e muet" (mute e): it counts as a syllable before a consonant, but it disappears (elides) before a vowel or at the very end of a line. Mastering this count is the first skill of prosody.

examples.french: Une rose pâlit sous la pluie
examples.english: A rose fades under the rain
examples.note: 9 syllables: u-ne / ro-se / pâ-lit / sous / la / plu-ie — the two mute e's before consonants both count

examples.french: Un soir d'automne, l'ombre arrive
examples.english: One autumn evening, the shadow arrives
examples.note: the e of "ombre" elides before the vowel of "arrive", so it does not count

examples.french: Elle marche seule dans la brume
examples.english: She walks alone in the mist
examples.note: the final e of "brume" is silent and never counted at all

examples.french: Le vent se lève et la mer gronde
examples.english: The wind rises and the sea rumbles
examples.note: 8 syllables — a working line for an octosyllabe

examples.french: J'écoute, immobile, le silence
examples.english: I listen, motionless, to the silence
examples.note: the final e of "silence" ends the line and is not counted

blocks.tip: Read the line aloud slowly: if you can feel a small extra beat before a consonant, that mute e is a syllable of the verse.

blocks.heading: L'alexandrin et les mètres classiques
blocks.body: The alexandrin — twelve syllables — is the grand line of French poetry, traditionally split into two equal halves of six syllables (hémistiches) by a pause called the césure. Shorter meters are common too: the octosyllabe (8 syllables) feels light and song-like, the décasyllabe (10) sits between the two.

examples.french: Le ciel est bleu, // la mer est calme et douce
examples.english: The sky is blue, // the sea is calm and sweet
examples.note: 12 syllables, 6+6 — the // marks the césure

examples.french: J'ai vu passer // l'ombre de ton visage
examples.english: I saw pass // the shadow of your face
examples.note: a regular alexandrin with the césure after the sixth syllable

examples.french: Le vent murmure au bord des toits
examples.english: The wind murmurs at the edge of the roofs
examples.note: 8 syllables — an octosyllabe

examples.french: Le fleuve coule sans jamais s'arrêter
examples.english: The river flows without ever stopping
examples.note: 10 syllables — a décasyllabe

examples.french: Sous le grand ciel d'hiver, // la ville dort encore
examples.english: Under the great winter sky, // the city still sleeps
examples.note: another alexandrin, césure after "hiver"

blocks.tip: Say the line and clap once on the sixth syllable of an alexandrin: that clap should fall on a natural pause in meaning, not mid-word.

blocks.heading: Les schémas de rimes
blocks.body: French poems arrange end-rhymes in three classic patterns: rimes plates (AABB, rhymes in couples), rimes croisées (ABAB, alternating), and rimes embrassées (ABBA, the outer pair "embracing" the inner one). Poets also alternate masculine rhymes (ending in a sounded consonant or vowel) with feminine rhymes (ending in a mute e) — a rule called the alternance.

examples.french: AABB — Il pleut sur la ville (A) / Un ciel immobile (A) / Le vent se repose (B) / Sur la terre morose (B)
examples.english: It rains on the town / A motionless sky / The wind rests / On the gloomy earth
examples.note: rimes plates: A-A-B-B

examples.french: ABAB — La lune monte (A) / Le fleuve dort (B) / Le monde compte (A) / Ses heures encore (B)
examples.english: The moon rises / The river sleeps / The world still counts / Its hours
examples.note: rimes croisées: A-B-A-B

examples.french: ABBA — Le soir descend (A) / Sur la vallée (B) / Toute voilée (B) / D'un bleu troublant (A)
examples.english: Evening falls / Over the valley / All veiled / In a disturbing blue
examples.note: rimes embrassées: A-B-B-A

blocks.tip: Mark each line-ending sound with a letter (A, B, C…) before you read further — the pattern becomes visible instantly.

blocks.heading: L'inversion poétique
blocks.body: To fit a meter or to place the emphatic word at the end of the line, French poets freely invert normal subject-verb order — something prose avoids outside of questions. Recognising this inversion is essential for understanding who does what in a poem.

examples.french: Vient le soir, et s'éteint la lumière.
examples.english: Evening comes, and the light goes out.
examples.note: normal order would be "Le soir vient" — inversion foregrounds "vient"

examples.french: Ainsi passent les jours, ainsi passe la vie.
examples.english: Thus the days pass, thus life passes.
examples.note: inversion after "ainsi" is common even outside poetry, but poets extend it further

examples.french: Au loin gronde la mer, immense et sombre.
examples.english: In the distance the sea rumbles, vast and dark.
examples.note: the adverbial phrase opens the line, verb comes before its subject

examples.french: Tombent les feuilles, lentes, sur le chemin.
examples.english: The leaves fall, slow, onto the path.
examples.note: verb-first opening gives the falling motion immediacy

blocks.tip: When a line opens with the verb, mentally move the verb after the noun that follows it — the meaning becomes prose-clear.

blocks.heading: Les licences poétiques
blocks.body: Poets sometimes bend everyday grammar to fit the syllable count or to sound archaic and elevated. Common licences include shortened forms like "encor" for "encore" (saves one syllable), and dropping "ne" in a negation when the meter demands it — something strictly forbidden in standard written French.

examples.french: Il fait encor nuit sur la ville endormie.
examples.english: It is still night over the sleeping town.
examples.note: "encor" instead of "encore" removes one syllable

examples.french: Je ne sais plus rien, je n'espère guère.
examples.english: I no longer know anything, I hardly hope.
examples.note: "guère" alone (without "ne... guère" fully spelled) is standard, but poets may drop "ne" entirely for rhythm

examples.french: Rien ne bouge, pas un souffle, pas un bruit.
examples.english: Nothing moves, not a breath, not a sound.
examples.note: the repeated "pas un" mimics a poetic rather than everyday register

examples.french: Qu'importe le temps qui passe et qui s'enfuit ?
examples.english: What does the passing, fleeting time matter?
examples.note: "qu'importe" is a fixed poetic/literary turn of phrase, rare in ordinary speech

blocks.tip: Treat "encor", "avecque", or a missing "ne" as signals that you are reading verse in an elevated, slightly older register — not errors.

passages.title: Apprendre à scander
passages.french:
Il a fallu à Sophie plusieurs semaines avant de sentir, sous les mots, le battement caché des vers.
Son professeur répétait la même consigne : compter, toujours compter, avant de juger un poème réussi ou raté.
Elle commença par les alexandrins, ces lignes de douze syllabes que la tradition tient pour les plus nobles.
Au début, elle butait sur chaque e muet, incapable de décider s'il fallait le prononcer ou le taire.
Peu à peu, elle comprit la règle : sonore devant une consonne, silencieux devant une voyelle ou en fin de vers.
La césure, elle aussi, lui parut d'abord un obstacle plutôt qu'un repère.
Puis un soir, en lisant à voix haute, elle sentit la pause naturelle tomber exactement à la moitié du vers.
« C'est comme une respiration », lui dit son professeur, « le poète vous indique où souffler. »
Elle s'attaqua ensuite aux schémas de rimes, notant patiemment les lettres A, B, C dans la marge.
Les rimes plates lui semblèrent d'abord trop simples, presque enfantines dans leur régularité.
Les rimes croisées, en revanche, exigeaient une mémoire plus longue : il fallait garder le premier son en tête jusqu'au troisième vers.
Quant aux rimes embrassées, elles lui donnèrent l'impression que la strophe se refermait sur elle-même, comme une parenthèse.
Elle découvrit aussi que certains poètes, pour respecter le compte, s'autorisaient des licences : un « encor » plutôt qu'un « encore », une inversion inattendue du sujet.
Ce qui la fascina le plus, néanmoins, ce fut de constater qu'une contrainte aussi stricte pouvait produire une telle liberté d'émotion.
Elle qui pensait la forme ennemie du sens comprit alors qu'elle en était, au contraire, l'un des instruments les plus fins.
Depuis, quand elle lit un poème, ses lèvres comptent sans qu'elle s'en aperçoive, et le vers, enfin, chante pour elle.
passages.english:
It took Sophie several weeks before she could feel, beneath the words, the hidden beat of the verses.
Her teacher repeated the same instruction: count, always count, before judging a poem successful or flawed.
She began with alexandrines, those twelve-syllable lines that tradition holds to be the noblest.
At first, she stumbled over every mute e, unable to decide whether to pronounce it or leave it silent.
Little by little, she understood the rule: sounded before a consonant, silent before a vowel or at the end of a line.
The caesura, too, seemed at first an obstacle rather than a landmark.
Then one evening, reading aloud, she felt the natural pause fall exactly at the middle of the line.
"It's like breathing," her teacher told her, "the poet is showing you where to breathe."
She then tackled rhyme schemes, patiently noting the letters A, B, C in the margin.
Flat rhymes seemed at first too simple, almost childish in their regularity.
Crossed rhymes, on the other hand, demanded a longer memory: you had to keep the first sound in mind until the third line.
As for embraced rhymes, they gave her the impression that the stanza closed in on itself, like a parenthesis.
She also discovered that certain poets, to respect the count, allowed themselves licences: an "encor" rather than an "encore", an unexpected inversion of the subject.
What fascinated her most, however, was noticing that such a strict constraint could produce such freedom of emotion.
She who thought form was the enemy of meaning then understood that it was, on the contrary, one of its finest instruments.
Since then, when she reads a poem, her lips count without her noticing, and the line, at last, sings for her.

questions.prompt: What did Sophie discover the pause in the middle of the alexandrine to be?

What conclusion does Sophie ultimately reach about poetic form?
options: It is, contrary to what she thought, one of the finest instruments of meaning
It is an outdated obstacle that modern poets should abandon
It matters less than the poet's choice of vocabulary
It only matters for very long poems
questions.answer: It is, contrary to what she thought, one of the finest instruments of meaning

lessons.title: Les images poétiques
lessons.description: Explore how metaphor and personification work specifically inside verse, shaping meaning through sound and image.

blocks.heading: La métaphore au service du vers
blocks.body: In poetry, a metaphor does more than compare two things without "comme" or "tel que" — it must also fit the line's rhythm and often carries the rhyme itself. A single well-placed metaphoric noun can close a verse and unlock the whole stanza's meaning at once.

examples.french: La lune est une perle posée sur l'eau noire.
examples.english: The moon is a pearl set upon the black water.
examples.note: the metaphor "une perle" also lands on the strong final position of the line

examples.french: Ses yeux, deux lacs profonds, gardaient tous ses silences.
examples.english: Her eyes, two deep lakes, held all her silences.
examples.note: the metaphor is inserted between commas, keeping the syllable count intact

examples.french: Le temps, ce fleuve sourd, emporte nos années.
examples.english: Time, that deaf river, carries away our years.
examples.note: an apposition metaphor — "ce fleuve sourd" renames "le temps"

examples.french: L'hiver a refermé son poing sur le jardin.
examples.english: Winter has closed its fist over the garden.
examples.note: the metaphor "son poing" personifies winter while staying purely metaphorical

blocks.tip: In verse, look for the noun placed right before the rhyme — poets often save their strongest image for that position.

blocks.heading: La personnification et le monde animé
blocks.body: Personification gives human traits — a gesture, a voice, an intention — to something that has none: the wind, the night, the sea. In poetry, this device is rarely decorative; it turns the landscape into a silent character that watches, waits, or suffers alongside the speaker.

examples.french: Le vent se plaint aux volets fermés.
examples.english: The wind complains at the closed shutters.
examples.note: "se plaint" gives the wind a human voice of complaint

examples.french: La nuit pose sa main froide sur la ville.
examples.english: The night lays its cold hand upon the town.
examples.note: "sa main" personifies the night as a physical, gesturing presence

examples.french: La mer, patiente, attend le retour des pêcheurs.
examples.english: The sea, patient, awaits the fishermen's return.
examples.note: the adjective "patiente" attributes a human virtue to the sea

examples.french: Le vieux mur se souvient encore des voix d'enfants.
examples.english: The old wall still remembers the voices of children.
examples.note: "se souvient" grants the wall a human memory

blocks.tip: Ask who or what is performing the verb: if it is normally incapable of that action, personification is at work.

blocks.heading: Quand l'image porte le sens du poème
blocks.body: In prose, an image often illustrates an idea already stated elsewhere. In poetry, the image frequently is the idea — there is no separate explanation to fall back on. Learning to read C1-level verse means learning to extract meaning directly from metaphor and personification, without waiting for the poet to spell it out.

examples.french: Elle portait son chagrin comme une pierre au fond de la poche.
examples.english: She carried her sorrow like a stone at the bottom of her pocket.
examples.note: the comparison alone conveys the weight and hiddenness of grief — nothing else is said

examples.french: Le silence entre eux avait grandi, avait pris toute la pièce.
examples.english: The silence between them had grown, had taken over the whole room.
examples.note: personifying silence as something that "grows" replaces a direct statement of estrangement

examples.french: Ses mots tombaient, feuilles mortes, sur un cœur d'hiver.
examples.english: Her words fell, dead leaves, onto a heart of winter.
examples.note: two images stacked together — "feuilles mortes" and "cœur d'hiver" — do the emotional work of a whole paragraph

blocks.tip: When a poem seems to say very little, look for what its images are doing instead of its statements.

blocks.heading: L'apposition poétique
blocks.body: Poets often rename a noun with a second noun phrase set off by commas — no "comme", no verb, just apposition. This compresses a full metaphor into a few words without breaking the line's syllable count, and it forces the reader to hold both images at once.

examples.french: Le temps, ce fleuve sourd, emporte nos années.
examples.english: Time, that deaf river, carries away our years.
examples.note: "ce fleuve sourd" is in apposition to "le temps" — no linking verb needed

examples.french: La lune, lampe pâle, éclaire le jardin.
examples.english: The moon, pale lamp, lights the garden.
examples.note: the apposition "lampe pâle" replaces an entire comparative clause

examples.french: Ses mots, feuilles mortes, tombaient sur le silence.
examples.english: Her words, dead leaves, fell upon the silence.
examples.note: two nouns stand side by side; the second reinterprets the first

examples.french: Paris, ville de pierre, ne dort jamais tout à fait.
examples.english: Paris, city of stone, never quite sleeps.
examples.note: apposition also works with longer noun phrases introduced by "de"

blocks.tip: When you see a noun immediately followed by a comma and another noun phrase, read it as "which is/are" — it is a compressed metaphor.

blocks.heading: Le présent de vérité poétique
blocks.body: When a poet personifies the wind, the sea, or the night, the verb is almost always in the present tense — not to describe a single passing moment, but to state something felt as timelessly true within the poem's world. This "present of poetic truth" resembles the gnomic present of proverbs, but applies it to invented, imagined actions.

examples.french: Le vent se plaint aux volets fermés.
examples.english: The wind complains at the closed shutters.
examples.note: present tense presents this as an ongoing, almost eternal habit of the wind, not a one-time event

examples.french: La mer, patiente, attend le retour des pêcheurs.
examples.english: The sea, patient, awaits the fishermen's return.
examples.note: the sea's waiting is framed as a permanent condition, like a proverb

examples.french: Le vieux mur se souvient encore des voix d'enfants.
examples.english: The old wall still remembers the voices of children.
examples.note: the present of "se souvient" gives the memory a lasting, unchanging quality

examples.french: L'hiver referme son poing sur le jardin.
examples.english: Winter closes its fist over the garden.
examples.note: present tense turns a seasonal image into a recurring, almost ritual gesture

blocks.tip: Do not translate this present as "is doing right now" — read it as "this is simply how it is", the way you would read a proverb.

passages.title: Nocturne au jardin
passages.french:
La nuit pose sa main froide sur la ville endormie,
et chaque réverbère s'allume comme un œil qui refuse de dormir.
Le vent se plaint aux volets fermés,
il raconte, à qui veut l'entendre, l'histoire d'un été perdu.
La lune, lampe pâle, éclaire le jardin désert
où l'automne a signé, sur chaque banc, une lettre de feuilles mortes.
Le vieux mur se souvient encore des voix d'enfants,
il les garde, patient, sous sa peau de pierre fendue.
Le temps, ce fleuve sourd, emporte nos années
sans jamais nous demander la permission de partir.
Au loin, la mer attend le retour d'un bateau,
et compte, sur ses vagues, les jours qui ne reviendront pas.
Une voix, quelque part, tombait comme une feuille sur un cœur d'hiver,
et le silence, entre deux ombres, avait pris toute la place.
Pourtant, à l'est, une aube se prépare déjà,
discrète, patiente, comme une promesse qu'on n'ose pas encore nommer.
passages.english:
The night lays its cold hand upon the sleeping town,
and every streetlamp lights up like an eye that refuses to sleep.
The wind complains at the closed shutters,
it tells, to whoever will listen, the story of a lost summer.
The moon, pale lamp, lights the deserted garden
where autumn has signed, on every bench, a letter of dead leaves.
The old wall still remembers the voices of children,
it keeps them, patient, beneath its cracked skin of stone.
Time, that deaf river, carries away our years
without ever asking our permission to leave.
Far off, the sea awaits the return of a boat,
and counts, on its waves, the days that will not come back.
A voice, somewhere, fell like a leaf onto a heart of winter,
and the silence, between two shadows, took up all the room.
And yet, in the east, a dawn is already preparing itself,
discreet, patient, like a promise no one yet dares to name.

lessons.title: Lire un poème
lessons.description: Read, analyse, and compose short original poems, bringing together metre, rhyme, and image.

blocks.heading: Lire un poème à voix haute
blocks.body: Reading a poem well means respecting punctuation, not the line break. When a sentence spills over the end of a line without a comma or period — an enjambment — you should not pause; let your voice carry through to where the syntax actually stops.

examples.french: Elle marchait sans but, cherchant peut-être un signe / que la vie n'avait pas oublié de lui laisser.
examples.english: She walked aimlessly, perhaps searching for a sign / that life had not forgotten to leave her.
examples.note: no pause at the end of the first line — the sentence continues straight into the second

examples.french: Le fleuve, lentement, / se retire vers la mer.
examples.english: The river, slowly, / withdraws toward the sea.
examples.note: here the comma DOES ask for a short pause, even mid-line

examples.french: Il n'a jamais su dire / ce que ce silence voulait dire.
examples.english: He never knew how to say / what that silence meant.
examples.note: another enjambment: read straight through, only breathing at the final period

blocks.tip: Before reading aloud, mark every comma, period, and question mark in pencil — those, not the line endings, tell you where to breathe.

blocks.heading: Interpréter avant de juger
blocks.body: Before deciding what a poem "means", identify three things in order: its form (meter, rhyme scheme, stanza shape), its dominant images, and only then its likely theme. Jumping straight to interpretation often leads readers to project a meaning the text does not actually support.

examples.french: D'abord la forme : trois quatrains en alexandrins, rimes croisées.
examples.english: First the form: three quatrains in alexandrines, crossed rhymes.
examples.note: always start by naming what you can measure

examples.french: Ensuite les images : la mer revient trois fois, toujours associée à l'attente.
examples.english: Then the images: the sea returns three times, always associated with waiting.
examples.note: count recurring images before interpreting them

examples.french: Enfin, le thème possible : le poème semble parler du temps qui passe sans qu'on l'ait choisi.
examples.english: Finally, the possible theme: the poem seems to speak of time passing without our choosing it.
examples.note: the theme is proposed as a hypothesis, grounded in form and image, not asserted as fact

blocks.tip: If you cannot point to a specific line supporting your interpretation, treat it as a guess, not a conclusion.

blocks.heading: Composer un poème court
blocks.body: To write a short original poem, start from a single concrete image rather than an abstract idea — a closed window, a cold cup of coffee, a departing train. Choose a form (regular verse or vers libre), then let the image generate a metaphor or a personification, and revise until the rhythm feels natural when read aloud.

examples.french: Une tasse refroidit sur la table vide.
examples.english: A cup grows cold on the empty table.
examples.note: a concrete starting image, deliberately simple

examples.french: Elle attend, patiente, qu'on se souvienne d'elle.
examples.english: It waits, patient, for someone to remember it.
examples.note: personifying the cup extends the image into a small poem

examples.french: Dehors, le train siffle une dernière fois.
examples.english: Outside, the train whistles one last time.
examples.note: a second image widens the scene without abandoning the first

blocks.tip: Write a plain-prose version of your idea first, then cut every word that is not doing real work — poetry is prose with nothing to spare.

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel de l'hypothèse interprétative
blocks.body: When proposing a reading of a poem, careful C1 writers use the conditional rather than the indicative — it signals "this is one possible interpretation", not an established fact. Phrases like "on pourrait y voir", "il s'agirait de", and "ce vers évoquerait" keep the analysis appropriately tentative.

examples.french: On pourrait y voir une image de la solitude.
examples.english: One might see in it an image of solitude.
examples.note: conditional "pourrait" signals a proposed, not certain, reading

examples.french: Ce silence évoquerait, selon certains critiques, la peur de l'oubli.
examples.english: This silence would evoke, according to some critics, the fear of being forgotten.
examples.note: the conditional distances the claim from the writer's own certainty

examples.french: Il s'agirait moins d'un poème d'amour que d'un poème sur le temps.
examples.english: It would be less a love poem than a poem about time.
examples.note: conditional "s'agirait" softens what is still a strong claim

examples.french: La lune serait ici le symbole d'une présence absente.
examples.english: The moon would here be the symbol of an absent presence.
examples.note: conditional "serait" invites the reader to weigh the claim rather than accept it outright

blocks.tip: Switching your interpretation from the conditional to the indicative is itself a rhetorical move — it says "I am now certain", so use it sparingly.

blocks.heading: L'impératif pour composer
blocks.body: Writing exercises and poetic workshops in French often instruct in the imperative — the tu or vous form of the verb with no subject pronoun. This direct, encouraging register ("Choisis une image", "Notez ce que vous ressentez") is standard in creative-writing prompts and appears throughout French poetry manuals.

examples.french: Choisis une image concrète avant d'écrire le premier vers.
examples.english: Choose a concrete image before writing the first line.
examples.note: tu-imperative, typical of informal workshop instructions

examples.french: Notez ce que vous ressentez, sans encore chercher la rime.
examples.english: Write down what you feel, without yet looking for the rhyme.
examples.note: vous-imperative, more formal register for a written guide

examples.french: Relis ton poème à voix haute et coupe ce qui ne sonne pas juste.
examples.english: Read your poem aloud again and cut what doesn't sound right.
examples.note: the imperative here gives concrete, actionable advice

examples.french: N'explique pas ton image : laisse-la agir seule.
examples.english: Don't explain your image: let it act alone.
examples.note: negative imperative — note "ne... pas" wraps directly around the verb

blocks.tip: In workshop instructions, tu signals a personal, encouraging tone; vous signals a more formal manual — choose consistently within one text.

passages.title: Le train du soir
passages.french:
Le train du soir s'éloigne, et personne ne sait
dire au juste pourquoi son sifflet nous poursuit ;
il emporte, entrelacés, ceux qui restaient
et ceux qui partent enfin sans faire de bruit.
Sur le quai désert, une aube se prépare,
discrète, patiente, entre deux réverbères ;
le murmure du rail, longtemps, se sépare
du silence, et s'en va rejoindre la lumière.
On dirait que le temps tisse, à chaque seconde,
un fil trop fin pour qu'on le voie jamais ;
il faudrait plus qu'un vers pour dire à quel point
cet instant fugace ressemble à l'infini.
Alors on reste là, sans bagage et sans hâte,
à compter les wagons qui glissent, un à un,
et l'on comprend, trop tard, que rien ne se répète —
que chaque adieu, pourtant, ressemble à un autre.
passages.english:
The evening train pulls away, and no one really knows
how to say why its whistle follows us;
it carries off, intertwined, those who stayed
and those who finally leave without a sound.
On the empty platform, a dawn is preparing itself,
discreet, patient, between two streetlamps;
the murmur of the rail, for a long while, separates
from the silence, and goes off to join the light.
One would say that time weaves, every second,
a thread too fine ever to be seen;
it would take more than a single line to say how much
this fleeting instant resembles the infinite.
So we stay there, without luggage, without hurry,
counting the carriages sliding by, one by one,
and we understand, too late, that nothing repeats itself —
that every farewell, still, resembles another.
